notes.meaning: Moses' own sister and brother, Miriam and Aaron, spoke against him. They used his foreign wife as the excuse, but the real reason seems to have been jealousy of his power and authority. Miriam is named first because she most likely started the quarrel and drew Aaron in. Many of these writers think the wife was Zipporah, called a 'Cushite' because the name covered peoples of Arabia, perhaps said as an insult. Others think Moses had married again after Zipporah died.

Aaron and Miriam had both been given the gift of prophecy, so they wanted an equal share in leading. They were proud of a gift that should have made them humble, since it came freely from God. 'The LORD heard this' means God took notice, ready to act as Judge.

This short note explains why Moses said nothing back and did not even ask God to punish them. He was gentle and patient, so he left his cause with God. He was bold as a lion for God's honor, but mild as a lamb when only his own honor was hurt. The line is not bragging; it shows why God stepped in, and it teaches us to wait quietly for God when we are wronged.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critics say a truly humble man would not write this about himself. They use the verse as an argument that Moses did not write this book.

notes.meaning: God acted at once to stop the rebellion before it spread among the people. Calling all three to the Tent of Meeting brought them into God's holy presence. There they would be reminded that they must answer to Him.

God came down in the cloud and stood at the entrance, like a judge sitting at the city gate to hear a case. Aaron and Miriam were called forward on their own, apart from Moses, like people on trial. God meeting them outside, rather than letting Aaron in as usual, was a sign He was displeased.
God explains that there are differences among prophets. With ordinary prophets He makes Himself known through visions and dreams. These were the two usual ways He spoke to them.

Moses is different. God had set him over 'all My house,' meaning all of Israel, God's people. He had proved faithful and trustworthy in that great work. The book of Hebrews quotes this to show that Jesus is greater still: Moses was faithful as a servant, but Christ as a Son.

God spoke with Moses 'face to face,' plainly and closely, the way friends talk. This clarity mattered because Moses was receiving God's laws, which had to be easy for everyone to understand. Seeing 'the form of the LORD' does not mean seeing God's full being, which no one can see and live. It means a clear sign of His glorious presence. So Aaron and Miriam should have been afraid to speak against such a servant.

God was angry with them and left, like a judge leaving the court after giving the sentence. He did not wait to hear excuses, since He already knew their hearts. Losing God's presence is the surest and saddest sign of His displeasure.

As the cloud lifted, Miriam was struck with leprosy, a serious skin disease that made a person unclean and cut off from others. Its sudden, snow-white form showed it was a judgment from God. Miriam was struck and Aaron was not, likely because she led the quarrel, and because disgrace on the high priest would have harmed God's worship. As priest, Aaron had to look at her and see the disease, knowing he was just as guilty.

Aaron, shaken by what happened to his sister, now humbly calls his younger brother 'my lord.' He admits plainly that they sinned and acted foolishly. Since Moses was the one they had wronged, Aaron asks his forgiveness. This is what true repentance (turning back from sin) looks like.

Aaron paints a painful picture: a baby born dead with its flesh already wasting away. He compares Miriam to this because the disease was eating away her living body. He describes her misery to move Moses to pity.

Moses does not hold a grudge. He cries out at once for God to heal the very sister who had insulted him. This proves how gentle he was. It shows us how to pray for those who hurt us, as Jesus did when He said, 'Father, forgive them.'

God answers the prayer, but not without shame. If a father spat in his daughter's face to show his anger, she would hide away in shame for a week. So Miriam must stay outside the camp seven days, then be brought back. Mercy and justice meet here: she is healed, but she bears public shame as a warning to all.

The whole camp waited for Miriam before moving on. This was a kindness to her, so she would not be crushed by shame or looked down on as a prophetess. It also reminded the people that sin holds back God's people on their journey.

Once Miriam was back, Israel moved from Hazeroth to the Wilderness of Paran. This was near Kadesh, at the southern edge of the promised land, where the spies would be sent out next. They could have entered the land soon, but their own sins would turn a short trip into many years of wandering.
